beats.intro: Chapter two. [[sub]]Before we can analyze data, we need to organize it, picture it, and describe it with a few numbers.
beats.types: [[root]]Data comes in two broad kinds. [[num]]Numerical data are numbers. [[disc]]Discrete numbers can be counted, like the number of trades. [[cont]]Continuous numbers can take any value in a range, like a stock price. [[cat]]Categorical data are labels. [[nom]]Nominal categories have no order, like a company's sector. [[ord]]Ordinal categories can be ranked, like a credit rating. [[end]]The kind of data decides which statistics make sense.
beats.shapes: [[a]]Data also differ in how they are collected. [[cs]]Cross-sectional data look at many entities at a single point in time, such as the returns of six companies this month. [[ts]]Time-series data follow one entity across many dates, such as one company's returns over six months. [[panel]]Panel data combine both: many entities, each followed over time.
beats.freq: [[dots]]Here are twenty monthly returns. A list like this is hard to read. [[drop]]Sort them into intervals of equal width. [[bars]]The height of each bar is the absolute frequency: how many observations fall in the interval. [[tall]]The tallest interval, zero to two percent, holds six observations. [[rel]]Divide by twenty and we get the relative frequency: thirty percent of the months. This picture is a histogram.
beats.charts: [[a]]Which chart should you pick? Start with the question you want answered. [[c1]]To see how values are distributed, use a histogram. [[c2]]To compare categories, use a bar chart. [[c3]]To follow a value over time, use a line chart. [[c4]]To see how two variables move together, use a scatter plot. [[end]]Tree-maps, word clouds and heat maps serve more specialized jobs, but the rule is the same: match the chart to the question.
beats.mean: [[dots]]Here are five values. [[mean]]The mean is the balance point: the sum, twenty, divided by five, gives four. [[median]]The median is the middle value after sorting: three. [[mode]]The mode is the most frequent value: three. [[outlier]]Now one value jumps to twenty-eight. The mean is dragged up to eight, but the median stays at three. [[note]]When outliers are present, the median is the more robust measure of the center.
beats.geo: [[a]]Averaging returns needs care. [[y1]]Start with one hundred dollars. A ten percent gain makes it one hundred ten. [[y2]]A ten percent loss then leaves ninety-nine. [[arith]]The arithmetic mean of plus ten and minus ten is zero, which suggests no change. But we lost a dollar. [[geo]]The geometric mean multiplies the growth factors, one point one times point nine, takes the square root, and subtracts one. That gives about minus point five percent per year, which matches what really happened.
beats.harmonic: [[a]]The harmonic mean suits averaging prices when you invest the same amount each time. [[b1]]Spend one thousand dollars at ten dollars a share: one hundred shares. [[b2]]Spend another thousand at twenty dollars: fifty shares. [[tot]]Two thousand dollars bought one hundred fifty shares, an average cost of thirteen dollars thirty-three. [[cmp]]That is the harmonic mean. The arithmetic mean, fifteen dollars, would overstate the cost.
beats.quantiles: [[a]]Quantiles split sorted data into equal parts. Here are eleven sorted values. [[pos]]The position of the p-th percentile is n plus one, times p over one hundred. [[med]]For the median, that is position six: the value is twelve. [[q1]]For the first quartile, position three: six. [[q3]]For the third quartile, position nine: eighteen. [[iqr]]The distance between the quartiles, the interquartile range, is twelve. It holds the middle half of the data.
beats.spread: [[a]]Dispersion measures how spread out data are. Take five values with a mean of six. [[range]]The range is the largest minus the smallest: eight. [[dev]]Each value sits some distance from the mean. [[mad]]Averaging the absolute distances gives the mean absolute deviation: two point four. [[var]]Squaring the distances and adding gives forty. Divide by n minus one, which is four, for the sample variance: ten. [[sd]]Its square root, the sample standard deviation, is about three point one six, back in the original units.
beats.q2: Quick check. Find the sample variance.
beats.cv: [[a]]Which fund has the better trade-off? [[fa]]Fund A earns ten percent on average with a standard deviation of fifteen. [[fb]]Fund B earns six percent with a standard deviation of six. [[cv]]The coefficient of variation divides the standard deviation by the mean: risk per unit of return. A is one point five, B is one. Lower is better, so B is the more efficient. [[dd]]Standard deviation counts ups and downs alike. Downside deviation measures only the results below a chosen target.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Know your data type: numerical or categorical, cross-sectional, time-series or panel. [[w2]]Frequency distributions and the right chart reveal the shape of data. [[w3]]Mean, median and mode locate the center. The median resists outliers; the geometric mean fits returns. [[w4]]Range, variance, standard deviation and the coefficient of variation measure spread. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of chapter two.
